claim: Classical G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling takes place in response to extracellular stimuli and involves receptors and heterotrimeric G proteins located at the plasma membrane.
source: Classical G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling takes place in response to extracellular stimuli and involves receptors and heterotrimeric G proteins located at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GPCR signaling mechanisms.

claim: GPCR signaling can take place from intracellular membrane compartments, including endosomes that contain internalized receptors and ligands.
source: It has recently been established that GPCR signaling can also take place from intracellular membrane compartments, including endosomes that contain internalized receptors and ligands.
evidence: This statement references recent scientific consensus about intracellular GPCR signaling.

claim: The mechanisms of GPCR endocytosis are well understood.
source: While the mechanisms of GPCR endocytosis are well understood, it is not clear how well internalized receptors are supplied with G proteins.
evidence: This reflects established scientific knowledge about GPCR endocytosis.

claim: It is not clear how well internalized receptors are supplied with G proteins.
source: While the mechanisms of GPCR endocytosis are well understood, it is not clear how well internalized receptors are supplied with G proteins.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Constitutive endocytosis is sufficient to supply newly internalized endocytic vesicles with 20–30% of the G protein density found at the plasma membrane.
source: We show here that constitutive endocytosis is sufficient to supply newly internalized endocytic vesicles with 20–30% of the G protein density found at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 4).

claim: G proteins are present on early, late, and recycling endosomes.
source: We find that G proteins are present on early, late, and recycling endosomes, are abundant on lysosomes, but are virtually undetectable on the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, and the medial-trans Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is supported by imaging and BRET data shown in Figure 3.

claim: G proteins are abundant on lysosomes.
source: We find that G proteins are present on early, late, and recycling endosomes, are abundant on lysosomes, but are virtually undetectable on the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, and the medial-trans Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: G proteins are virtually undetectable on the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, and the medial-trans Golgi apparatus.
source: We find that G proteins are present on early, late, and recycling endosomes, are abundant on lysosomes, but are virtually undetectable on the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, and the medial-trans Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Receptor activation does not change heterotrimer abundance on endosomes.
source: Receptor activation does not change heterotrimer abundance on endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by BRET data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: G proteins may be partially excluded from nascent endocytic vesicles.
source: Our findings provide a subcellular map of endogenous G protein distribution, suggest that G proteins may be partially excluded from nascent endocytic vesicles, and are likely to have implications for GPCR signaling from endosomes and other intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing lower G protein density on endocytic vesicles compared to the plasma membrane.

claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins transduce a vast number of important physiological signals.
source: Heterotrimeric G proteins transduce a vast number of important physiological signals (Gilman, 1987), most often in response to activation by G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs; Pierce et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Canonical G protein signaling occurs when a cell surface GPCR is activated by an extracellular ligand, which in turn promotes activation of plasma membrane G protein heterotrimers and downstream effectors.
source: Canonical G protein signaling occurs when a cell surface GPCR is activated by an extracellular ligand, which in turn promotes activation of plasma membrane G protein heterotrimers and downstream effectors.
evidence: This describes established knowledge about canonical GPCR signaling.

claim: GPCRs can signal from intracellular compartments.
source: Recently, it has become clear that GPCRs can also signal from intracellular compartments (Calebiro et al., 2010; Eichel and von Zastrow, 2018), most notably endosomes and the Golgi apparatus (Calebiro et al., 2009; Ferrandon et al., 2009; Irannejad et al., 2017; Irannejad et al., 2013; Mullershausen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Signaling from endosomes is often a continuation of signaling that starts at the plasma membrane and persists as (or resumes after) active receptors are endocytosed.
source: Signaling from endosomes is often a continuation of signaling that starts at the plasma membrane and persists as (or resumes after) active receptors are endocytosed (Tsvetanova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: At least one isoform of the G protein effector adenylyl cyclase is actively internalized.
source: It is also known that at least one isoform of the G protein effector adenylyl cyclase is actively internalized (Lazar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Much less is known about how G protein heterotrimers traffic from the plasma membrane through intracellular compartments.
source: In contrast, much less is known about how G protein heterotrimers traffic from the plasma membrane through intracellular compartments (Wedegaertner, 2012).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: It is not known how efficiently heterotrimers are loaded onto endocytic vesicles at the plasma membrane.
source: It is not known how efficiently heterotrimers are loaded onto endocytic vesicles at the plasma membrane, how receptor activation might change this process, or what the fate of G proteins might be after endocytosis.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Activation at the plasma membrane promotes heterotrimer dissociation.
source: Activation at the plasma membrane promotes heterotrimer dissociation, and the resulting loss of membrane avidity allows Gβγ dimers and some Gα subunits (most notably Gαs) to translocate through the cytosol to sample intracellular membranes (Akgoz et al., 2004; Hynes et al., 2004; Ransnäs et al., 1989; Slepak and Hurley, 2008; Wedegaertner et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Activation-dependent translocation processes reverse quickly when activation ceases.
source: However, these processes reverse quickly when activation ceases (Akgoz et al., 2004; Martin and Lambert, 2016), meaning that activation-dependent translocation of free Gα subunits and Gβγ dimers would be an inefficient mechanism to deliver inactive heterotrimers to intracellular membranes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: G proteins have been detected on the surface of endosomes and other intracellular compartments using a variety of approaches.
source: G proteins have been detected on the surface of endosomes and other intracellular compartments using a variety of approaches (Hewavitharana and Wedegaertner, 2012; Irannejad et al., 2013; Scarselli and Donaldson, 2009; Wedegaertner, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: There has been no quantitative comparison of G protein distribution across identified subcellular compartments.
source: However, there has been no quantitative comparison of G protein distribution across identified subcellular compartments.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: Studies of endogenous G proteins are limited by the availability of well-validated antibodies suitable for immunostaining.
source: Studies of endogenous G proteins are limited by the availability of well-validated antibodies suitable for immunostaining, and overexpression of tagged G protein subunits may lead to aberrant localization.
evidence: This describes a methodological limitation in the field.

claim: Overexpression of tagged G protein subunits may lead to aberrant localization.
source: Studies of endogenous G proteins are limited by the availability of well-validated antibodies suitable for immunostaining, and overexpression of tagged G protein subunits may lead to aberrant localization.
evidence: This describes a methodological concern in the field.

claim: G proteins are abundant on membrane compartments that are functionally continuous with the plasma membrane, including early, late, and recycling endosomes.
source: We find that G proteins are abundant on membrane compartments that are functionally continuous with the plasma membrane, including early, late, and recycling endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by imaging and BRET data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Heterotrimer density on endocytic membranes is lower than on the plasma membrane.
source: However, heterotrimer density on endocytic membranes is lower than on the plasma membrane, suggesting that G protein endocytosis is inefficient.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: G protein endocytosis is inefficient.
source: However, heterotrimer density on endocytic membranes is lower than on the plasma membrane, suggesting that G protein endocytosis is inefficient.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing lower G protein density on endocytic vesicles.

claim: Endocytic trafficking of G proteins is not regulated by GPCRs.
source: Endocytic trafficking of G proteins is not regulated by GPCRs.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing no change in G protein distribution after receptor activation.

claim: Internalized receptors are concentrated in G-protein-deficient compartments.
source: Our findings are likely to have implications for GPCR signaling from endosomes, as internalized receptors are concentrated in G-protein-deficient compartments.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing lower G protein density on endosomes where receptors accumulate.

claim: Gβ1 is the most abundant Gβ subunit in HEK 293 cells.
source: We chose this subunit because it is the most abundant Gβ subunit in this cell type (Cho et al., 2022), it can associate with any type of Gα or Gγ subunit (Hillenbrand et al., 2015), and it can be labeled at this position without disrupting heterotrimer formation or function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Gβ1 can associate with any type of Gα or Gγ subunit.
source: We chose this subunit because it is the most abundant Gβ subunit in this cell type (Cho et al., 2022), it can associate with any type of Gα or Gγ subunit (Hillenbrand et al., 2015), and it can be labeled at this position without disrupting heterotrimer formation or function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Gβ1 can be labeled at the amino terminus without disrupting heterotrimer formation or function.
source: We chose this subunit because it is the most abundant Gβ subunit in this cell type (Cho et al., 2022), it can associate with any type of Gα or Gγ subunit (Hillenbrand et al., 2015), and it can be labeled at this position without disrupting heterotrimer formation or function.
evidence: This is supported by functional validation data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Amplicon sequencing verified that cell lines had correctly edited GNB1 genes.
source: Amplicon sequencing verified that cell lines had correctly edited GNB1 genes and SDS-PAGE revealed single proteins with apparent molecular weights consistent with edited Gβ1 subunits (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data described in the methods.

claim: SDS-PAGE revealed single proteins with apparent molecular weights consistent with edited Gβ1 subunits.
source: Amplicon sequencing verified that cell lines had correctly edited GNB1 genes and SDS-PAGE revealed single proteins with apparent molecular weights consistent with edited Gβ1 subunits (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tagged Gβ1 subunits in HiBit-β1 and mNG-β1 cell lines form functional heterotrimers with endogenous Gα and Gγ subunits.
source: BRET assays demonstrated that tagged subunits in HiBit-β1 and mNG-β1 cell lines formed functional heterotrimers with endogenous Gα and Gγ subunits.
evidence: This is supported by BRET data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Agonist-induced BRET was observed between the D2 dopamine receptor and mNG-β1.
source: For example, we observed agonist-induced BRET between the D2 dopamine receptor and mNG-β1, an interaction that requires association with endogenous Gα subunits (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by BRET data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: BRET was observed between HiBit-β1 and the free Gβγ sensor memGRKct-Venus after activation of receptors that couple Gi/o, Gs, and Gq heterotrimers.
source: Similarly, we observed BRET between HiBit-β1 and the free Gβγ sensor memGRKct-Venus after activation of receptors that couple Gi/o, Gs, and Gq heterotrimers, indicating that HiBit-β1 associated with endogenous Gα subunits from these three families (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by BRET data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cyclic AMP accumulation in response to stimulation of endogenous β adrenergic receptors was similar in edited cell lines and their unedited parent lines.
source: We also found that cyclic AMP accumulation in response to stimulation of endogenous β adrenergic receptors was similar in edited cell lines and their unedited parent lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP sensor data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous Gα and Gβ subunits are expressed at approximately a 1:1 ratio.
source: Endogenous Gα and Gβ subunits are expressed at approximately a 1:1 ratio, and Gβ subunits are tightly associated with Gγ and inactive Gα subunits (Cho et al., 2022; Gilman, 1987; Krumins and Gilman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gβ subunits are tightly associated with Gγ and inactive Gα subunits.
source: Endogenous Gα and Gβ subunits are expressed at approximately a 1:1 ratio, and Gβ subunits are tightly associated with Gγ and inactive Gα subunits (Cho et al., 2022; Gilman, 1987; Krumins and Gilman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Proteins that bind to free Gβγ dimers are found in the cytosol of unstimulated HEK 293 cells.
source: Moreover, proteins that bind to free Gβγ dimers are found in the cytosol of unstimulated HEK 293 cells, suggesting at most only a small population of free Gβγ in these cells (Barak et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Almost all mNG-β1 and HiBit-β1 subunits in unstimulated cells are part of heterotrimers.
source: Therefore, we assume that almost all mNG-β1 and HiBit-β1 subunits in unstimulated cells are part of heterotrimers.
evidence: This is inferred from the stoichiometry data and literature citations.

claim: Confocal imaging of mNG-β1 cells revealed bright fluorescence at the plasma membrane.
source: Confocal imaging of mNG-β1 cells revealed the expected bright fluorescence at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Most mNG-β1 cells contained pleiomorphic intracellular structures.
source: Most cells also contained pleiomorphic intracellular structures and dim cytosolic fluorescence that was sufficient to suggest relative exclusion of mNG-β1 from the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Clusters of large vesicular structures located at the cell periphery were identified as lysosomes.
source: Especially notable were clusters of large vesicular structures located at the cell periphery which were later identified as lysosomes (Figure 2A; see below).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A and later colocalization with lysosome markers in Figure 3.

claim: Large intracellular organelles such as the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, and Golgi apparatus were not evident in mNG-β1 imaging.
source: Large intracellular organelles such as the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, and Golgi apparatus were not evident.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: mNG-β1 does not colocalize with markers of the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, or medial-trans Golgi apparatus.
source: Markers of the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and medial-trans Golgi apparatus indicated that these large compartments were virtually devoid of mNG-β1 fluorescence (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization imaging data shown in Figure 2B-D and supplements.

claim: mNG-β1 clearly colocalizes with the marker FYVE, which binds to phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate (PI3P) on the surface of endosomes.
source: In contrast, mNG-β1 clearly colocalized with the marker FYVE, which binds to phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate (PI3P) on the surface of endosomes (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization imaging data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: mNG-β1 fluorescence was not detected on every FYVE-positive vesicle.
source: However, mNG-β1 fluorescence was not detected on every FYVE-positive vesicle and when present was much less intense than fluorescence of adjacent segments of the plasma membrane (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The median signal-to-background ratio for FYVE-positive structures was less than one-fourth that of the plasma membrane.
source: The median signal-to-background ratio for FYVE-positive structures was less than one-fourth that of the plasma membrane (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: FYVE domains primarily localize to early endosomes.
source: FYVE domains primarily localize to early endosomes (Hammond and Balla, 2015), so it was not surprising that similar colocalization of mNG-β1 was observed with the early endosome marker rab5a.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: mNG-β1 colocalized with the early endosome marker rab5a.
source: FYVE domains primarily localize to early endosomes (Hammond and Balla, 2015), so it was not surprising that similar colocalization of mNG-β1 was observed with the early endosome marker rab5a.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Dim mNG-β1 fluorescence was detected on indistinct rab11a-positive structures clustered diffusely in the vicinity of the nucleus.
source: Dim mNG-β1 fluorescence was detected on indistinct rab11a-positive structures clustered diffusely in the vicinity of the nucleus (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), which we presumptively identified as the perinuclear recycling compartment (PNRC).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: mNG-β1 colocalized extensively with vesicles labeled with rab7a, a marker of late endosomes.
source: Similarly, mNG-β1 colocalized extensively with vesicles labeled with rab7a, a marker of late endosomes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: mNG-β1 fluorescence was more intense on rab7a-positive late endosomes than on FYVE- or rab5a-positive early endosomes.
source: Notably, mNG-β1 fluorescence was more intense on rab7a-positive late endosomes than on FYVE- or rab5a-positive early endosomes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: mNG-β1 strongly colocalized with lysosomes marked with LysoView 633.
source: Accordingly, mNG-β1 strongly colocalized with lysosomes marked with LysoView 633 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 5), long-term incubation with fluorescent dextran (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), or the lysosome marker LAMP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A and supplements.

claim: Some mNG fluorescence was detected in the lumen of lysosomes.
source: While some mNG fluorescence was detected in the lumen of lysosomes, much of the signal remained on the cytosolic surface of these structures, and in many instances the intensity of mNG-β1 fluorescence on lysosomes was similar to that of the nearby plasma membrane (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Robust mNG-β1 signals were detected on structures labeled with TGNP, a marker of the trans-Golgi network.
source: We also detected robust mNG-β1 signals on structures labeled with TGNP (Figure 3—figure supplement 7), a marker of the trans-Golgi network.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: G proteins are likely to undergo endocytosis and enter both recycling and degradative pathways.
source: These imaging results suggest that G proteins are likely to undergo endocytosis and enter both recycling and degradative pathways and may become more concentrated as late endosomes mature.
evidence: This is inferred from the imaging data showing G proteins on early, late, and recycling endosomes as well as lysosomes.

claim: G proteins may become more concentrated as late endosomes mature.
source: These imaging results suggest that G proteins are likely to undergo endocytosis and enter both recycling and degradative pathways and may become more concentrated as late endosomes mature.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that G protein fluorescence is more intense on late endosomes than early endosomes.

claim: Bystander BRET experiments showed large signals at the plasma membrane, smaller signals at endosomes, and very small signals at the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria.
source: We expressed LgBit and a series of inert Venus-tagged membrane markers in HiBit-β1 cells and observed large bystander signals at the plasma membrane, smaller bystander signals at endosomes, and very small bystander signals at the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by BRET data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: mNG-β1 fluorescence was less intense on endosomes than the plasma membrane.
source: That mNG-β1 fluorescence was less intense on endosomes than the plasma membrane suggested that G protein density may be lower on the surface of endosomes than on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: FM4-64 rapidly and reversibly partitions into membranes and is only fluorescent in a hydrophobic environment.
source: To stain both the plasma membrane as well as newly formed endocytic vesicle membrane, we exposed live cells to the styryl dye FM4-64, which rapidly and reversibly partitions into (but does not cross) membranes and is only fluorescent in a hydrophobic environment (Betz et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature describing FM4-64 properties.

claim: When cells are exposed to FM4-64 at physiological temperatures the plasma membrane is stained immediately, followed by the appearance of intracellular vesicles that have trapped the dye.
source: When cells are exposed to FM4-64 at physiological temperatures the plasma membrane is stained immediately, and this is followed over the course of several minutes by the appearance of intracellular vesicles that have trapped the dye (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A and supplement.

claim: FM4-64 and CellMask dyes reported similar amounts of membrane surface area in endocytic vesicles.
source: After staining cells and allowing 15 min for constitutive endocytosis, we found that FM4-64 and CellMask dyes reported similar amounts of membrane surface area in endocytic vesicles (Figure 4A and B); in both cases, peak vesicle intensity was on average similar to the intensity of the plasma membrane (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Peak mNG-β1 fluorescence on endocytic vesicles was much less intense than the plasma membrane.
source: In contrast, peak mNG-β1 fluorescence on the same endocytic vesicles was much less intense than the plasma membrane (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: mNG-β1 density on FM4-64-positive vesicles was 20 ± 8% of the nearby plasma membrane.
source: Using FM4-64 fluorescence as a standard for membrane surface area, we calculated that mNG-β1 density on FM4-64-positive vesicles was 20 ± 8% (mean ± 95% CI; n=45) of the nearby plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: mNG-HRas ct was less abundant on FM4-64-positive endocytic vesicles than on the plasma membrane.
source: We found that mNG-HRas ct was also less abundant on FM4-64-positive endocytic vesicles than on the plasma membrane, although not to the same extent as mNG-β1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2); mNG-HRas ct density on FM4-64-positive vesicles was 64 ± 17% (mean ± 95% CI; n=78) of the nearby plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: SNAPf-β2AR was enriched approximately threefold on endocytic vesicles compared to the nearby plasma membrane.
source: Normalization and comparison to FM4-64 fluorescence indicated that SNAPf-β2AR was enriched approximately threefold on endocytic vesicles compared to the nearby plasma membrane (Figure 5B and C), consistent with active recruitment of active receptors to clathrin-coated pits and endocytic vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: mNG-β1 density on receptor-containing vesicles was 28 ± 8% of the nearby plasma membrane.
source: Using FM4-64 fluorescence as a standard for membrane surface area, we calculated that mNG-β1 density on receptor-containing vesicles was 28 ± 8% (mean ±95% CI; n=91) of the nearby plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The difference in mNG-β1 density between vesicles formed by constitutive endocytosis and receptor-containing vesicles did not reach significance.
source: Although this density was higher than that calculated for vesicles formed by constitutive endocytosis, the difference did not reach significance (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Activation-dependent internalization of β2 adrenergic receptors does not significantly promote or prevent loading of G proteins onto endocytic vesicles.
source: These results demonstrate that activation-dependent internalization of β2 adrenergic receptors does not significantly promote or prevent loading of G proteins onto endocytic vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing no significant difference in G protein density on vesicles with or without receptors.

claim: Small decreases in bystander BRET at the plasma membrane and small increases at intracellular compartments were observed during activation of GPCRs.
source: Consistent with this, we observed small decreases in bystander BRET at the plasma membrane and small increases in bystander BRET at intracellular compartments during activation of GPCRs, suggesting that endogenous Gβγ subunits undergo similar translocation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by BRET data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant changes in bystander BRET were observed at any endosome compartment after 30 min of receptor stimulation.
source: Under these conditions no significant changes in bystander BRET were observed at any endosome compartment after 30 min of receptor stimulation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by BRET data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Activation of receptors and G proteins does not substantially change heterotrimer abundance on the surface of endosomes.
source: Taken together these results indicate that activation of receptors and G proteins does not substantially change heterotrimer abundance on the surface of endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by BRET data shown in Figure 5E and supplements.

claim: Avoidance of endocytosis is likely to be important for maintaining a high density of heterotrimers at the plasma membrane.
source: Avoidance of endocytosis is likely to be important for maintaining a high density of heterotrimers at the plasma membrane, where much important signaling takes place.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that G proteins are inefficiently endocytosed.

claim: Inefficient G protein endocytosis limits the abundance of G proteins on the surface of endosomes.
source: On the other hand, this limits the abundance of G proteins on the surface of endosomes.
evidence: This is a direct consequence of the finding that G proteins are inefficiently endocytosed.

claim: Many endocytosis mechanisms rely on bulky coat proteins and adapters to induce membrane curvature and recruit cargo.
source: Many endocytosis mechanisms, including clathrin-mediated endocytosis, rely on bulky coat proteins and adapters to induce membrane curvature and recruit cargo (Doherty and McMahon, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins may be excluded from nascent endocytic vesicles by steric occlusion.
source: One possibility is that heterotrimeric G proteins are simply excluded from nascent endocytic vesicles by steric occlusion.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Large extracellular domains are known to impede endocytosis of membrane proteins.
source: While large extracellular domains are known to impede endocytosis of membrane proteins (DeGroot et al., 2018), a similar relationship has not been demonstrated for intracellular domains.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The monomeric G proteins HRas and NRas are less abundant on endosomes than the plasma membrane.
source: It is noteworthy that the monomeric G proteins HRas and NRas are also less abundant on endosomes than the plasma membrane, and therefore are separated from internalized growth factor receptors (Pinilla-Macua et al., 2016; Surve et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some studies using overexpressed G protein subunits have suggested that a large pool of G proteins is located on intracellular membranes, including the Golgi apparatus.
source: Some studies using overexpressed G protein subunits have suggested that a large pool of G proteins is located on intracellular membranes, including the Golgi apparatus (Chisari et al., 2007; Saini et al., 2007; Tsutsumi et al., 2009), whereas others have indicated a distribution that is dominated by the plasma membrane (Crouthamel et al., 2008; Evanko et al., 2000; Marrari et al., 2007; Takida and Wedegaertner, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neither Gα nor Gβγ traffic appropriately to the plasma membrane as free subunits.
source: A likely factor contributing to these discrepant results is the stoichiometry of overexpressed subunits, as neither Gα nor Gβγ traffic appropriately to the plasma membrane as free subunits (Wedegaertner, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Endogenous G proteins are primarily located on the plasma membrane and are present on internal membranes at substantially lower levels.
source: Our results show that endogenous G proteins are primarily located on the plasma membrane and are present on internal membranes at substantially lower levels.
evidence: This is supported by imaging and BRET data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Nascent heterotrimers are likely formed and lipid modified on the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus.
source: Nascent heterotrimers are likely formed and lipid modified on the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus (Wedegaertner, 2012), yet few heterotrimers can be found on these compartments at any given moment, consistent with a relatively slow rate of turnover compared to forward trafficking during biosynthesis (Gabay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: When Gβγ dimers are expressed alone they accumulate on the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Notably, when Gβγ dimers are expressed alone they accumulate on the endoplasmic reticulum (Michaelson et al., 2002; Takida and Wedegaertner, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Almost no endogenous Gβγ is detected on the endoplasmic reticulum, supporting the conclusion that the large majority of Gβγ in unstimulated HEK 293 cells is associated with Gα.
source: That we detect almost no endogenous Gβγ on the endoplasmic reticulum supports our conclusion that the large majority of Gβγ in unstimulated HEK 293 cells is associated with Gα.
evidence: This is inferred from the imaging data showing no G proteins on the ER.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated functional roles for G proteins on mitochondria.
source: Likewise, we found that few heterotrimers are associated with mitochondria, despite the fact that previous studies have demonstrated functional roles for G proteins on these organelles (Hewavitharana and Wedegaertner, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: GPCR signaling from intracellular compartments will generally have to be transduced by a lower density of G proteins.
source: Our results suggest that GPCR signaling from intracellular compartments will generally have to be transduced by a lower density of G proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that G protein density is lower on intracellular compartments.

claim: A recent large-scale study found that Gβ1 is enriched on the plasma membrane and lysosomes but is not significantly enriched on endosomes, the Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum, or mitochondria.
source: Consistent with these findings, a recent large-scale study assessing protein abundance on organelles in HEK 293 cells found that Gβ1 is enriched on the plasma membrane and lysosomes but is not significantly enriched on endosomes, the Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum, or mitochondria (Hein et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Fully lipid-modified heterotrimers in their inactive state are unlikely to detach from membranes at a significant rate.
source: Fully lipid-modified heterotrimers in their inactive state are unlikely to detach from membranes at a significant rate (Shahinian and Silvius, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Heterotrimers undergo vesicle-mediated endocytosis in unstimulated cells and are not efficiently sorted to either the slow recycling pathway or the degradative pathway.
source: Therefore, we infer from the presence of Gβ1 on early, late, and recycling endosomes that heterotrimers undergo vesicle-mediated endocytosis in unstimulated cells and are not efficiently sorted to either the slow recycling pathway or the degradative pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the imaging data showing G proteins on multiple endosome types.

claim: G proteins become concentrated as late endosomes mature.
source: Our imaging results also show that G proteins are apparently more abundant on late endosomes and lysosomes than on early endosomes, suggesting that they become concentrated as late endosomes mature.
evidence: This is inferred from the imaging data showing higher G protein fluorescence on late endosomes.

claim: Lysosomes may fuse with the plasma membrane under certain circumstances.
source: Since lysosomes may fuse with the plasma membrane under certain circumstances (Xu and Ren, 2015), it is possible that this represents a route of G protein recycling to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The results are largely consistent with the hypothesis that G proteins passively follow bulk endocytic flow of membrane.
source: Our results are largely consistent with the hypothesis that G proteins passively follow bulk endocytic flow of membrane and suggest that at least some G proteins are recycled to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing G proteins on multiple endosome types.

claim: At least some G proteins are recycled to the plasma membrane.
source: Our results are largely consistent with the hypothesis that G proteins passively follow bulk endocytic flow of membrane and suggest that at least some G proteins are recycled to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of G proteins on recycling endosomes.

claim: Tagging endogenous proteins with HiBit and other luciferase fragments has proven to be useful for studying several aspects of GPCR signaling.
source: Tagging endogenous proteins with HiBit and other luciferase fragments has proven to be useful for studying several aspects of GPCR signaling (White et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Subcellular localization of endogenous membrane proteins can be studied in living cells by adding a HiBit tag and performing bystander BRET mapping.
source: More broadly, our results show that subcellular localization of endogenous membrane proteins can be studied in living cells by adding a HiBit tag and performing bystander BRET mapping.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the methods and results presented in the study.

claim: Bystander BRET mapping has advantages over fluorescent protein complementation, notably the ability to localize endogenous membrane proteins that are expressed at levels too low to permit fluorescence microscopy.
source: Applied at large scale this approach would have some advantages over fluorescent protein complementation (Cho et al., 2022), most notably the ability to localize endogenous membrane proteins that are expressed at levels that are too low to permit fluorescence microscopy.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the two methods.

claim: The tags used to visualize and track G proteins may have had some influence on their trafficking.
source: Our labeling strategy was designed to interfere as little as possible with heterotrimer function, but we cannot rule out the possibility that the tags we used to visualize and track G proteins had some influence on their trafficking.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Labeling Gβ1 subunits does not allow direct distinction between heterotrimers and free Gβγ dimers.
source: By labeling Gβ1 subunits, we cannot directly distinguish heterotrimers from free Gβγ dimers, complicating interpretation.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Heterotrimers containing different Gα subunits could be subject to different trafficking mechanisms.
source: This strategy also does not allow us to resolve heterotrimers containing different Gα subunits. It is quite possible that heterotrimers containing different Gα subunits could be subject to different trafficking mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation about a limitation of the study.

claim: Other receptors may influence G protein distribution using mechanisms not shared by the receptors studied.
source: Our conclusion that GPCR activation has no lasting effect on the subcellular distribution of G proteins rests on three representative receptors, chosen because they activate three of the four major G protein families. It is possible that other receptors will influence G protein distribution using mechanisms not shared by the receptors we studied.
evidence: This is speculation about a limitation of the study.

claim: A few receptors are thought to form relatively stable complexes with Gβγ, which could provide a mechanism of trafficking to endosomes.
source: For example, a few receptors are thought to form relatively stable complexes with Gβγ, which could provide a mechanism of trafficking to endosomes (Thomsen et al., 2016; Wehbi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The study was limited to a single non-differentiated cell type.
source: Finally, our study was limited to a single non-differentiated cell type.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Differentiated cells may have mechanisms to regulate G protein trafficking and distribution that are not shared by the model cells used.
source: It would not be surprising to find that differentiated cells have mechanisms to regulate G protein trafficking and distribution that are not shared by the model cells we used (Calebiro et al., 2009; Kotowski et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2024; Puri et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins are more abundant on the plasma membrane than on any intracellular compartment where they are thought to be important for signaling.
source: In summary, here we show that heterotrimeric G proteins are more abundant on the plasma membrane than on any intracellular compartment where they are thought to be important for signaling.
evidence: This is supported by imaging and BRET data shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Receptor-G protein coupling is thought to be rate-limited by collision and G protein abundance.
source: Receptor-G protein coupling is thought to be rate-limited by collision and G protein abundance (Hein et al., 2005), and decreasing G protein expression is known to impair downstream signaling (Gabay et al., 2011; Schwindinger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Decreasing G protein expression is known to impair downstream signaling.
source: Receptor-G protein coupling is thought to be rate-limited by collision and G protein abundance (Hein et al., 2005), and decreasing G protein expression is known to impair downstream signaling (Gabay et al., 2011; Schwindinger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Signaling from endosomes and other compartments may be disadvantaged by a low density of G proteins.
source: Signaling from endosomes and other compartments may thus be disadvantaged by a low density of G proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that G protein density is lower on intracellular compartments.
